#10020. Announcing New vLLM and SGLang Inference Engines on TPU

As part of our broader announcements for PyTorch today, we are excited to launch native PyTorch backends for vLLM (developed in partnership with Inferact) and SGLang (developed in partnership with RadixArk).

For years, TPUs have powered large-scale AI workloads with high performance and efficiency. With the rise of agentic and multimodal workloads, serving efficiently is more important than ever. Both engines already run on TPU through JAX-based backends, but we kept hearing from developers that they wanted to customize and debug their serving stack in PyTorch.

So we started in earnest on TorchTPU, which runs PyTorch natively on TPU. We then built new vLLM and SGLang engines on top of it.

Our goal is for the PyTorch community to bring models to TPU and make them fast using the tools developers are already familiar with. The engines come with optimized, production-ready serving features and custom Pallas kernels.

Serving at scale requires co-design across every layer of the technology stack, from silicon to compilers to orchestration. Today's launch of new inference engines is at the central part of an integrated, open TPU ecosystem.

TorchTPU makes the TPU a native PyTorch device. Tensors are managed as standard PyTorch tensors on a tpu device with no wrapper types, code runs eagerly or compiles via torch.compile using XLA, and collectives go through torch.distributed.

Because each device runs its own PyTorch process, both engines keep each framework’s worker model, scheduler, KV cache manager, API server and so forth, with TPU implementations underneath.

Most models use the standard upstream PyTorch model definitions in both engines, with TPU-specific optimizations in kernels and layer implementations. Custom kernels written in Pallas are called directly from PyTorch as custom operators inside the compiled graph. This platform-plugin design reuses as much of each framework as possible while letting TPU optimizations move at their own pace.

Both engines are built for the full range of production workloads.

Agentic workloads in particular demand several of these features simultaneously. Because agents repeatedly resend expanding multi-turn conversations, serving them efficiently requires finding the cached prefix instead of recomputing it. Both engines keep reusable prefixes in HBM and, with host offload turned on, automatically move older prefixes to host memory as a second tier.

Two of these features move the KV cache away from the device that computed it. Disaggregated serving runs prefill and decode on separate TPU hosts, so each request's KV cache has to travel from the prefill host to the decode host.Tiered KV offload moves the part of the KV cache that no longer fits in HBM to the host's DRAM and secondary storage with Google Cloud Managed Lustre, and brings it back when a later request reuses the prefix. Either way, the transfer has to overlap computation or it adds directly to latency.

Both engines use TPU Sync for this. It is an open-source C++ library for KV cache transfer and management on TPU. It reads the device buffers behind PyTorch tensors directly, so a transfer needs no extra staging copy on the host, and it runs transfers on its own threads outside Python while prefill and decode continue. vLLM-TorchTPU exposes it through vLLM's KV connector interface. SGLang-TorchTPU uses it as a disaggregation transfer backend and as the I/O backend for HiCache.

Both engines are already running at scale in production with preview customers. To provide transparent, reproducible proof of our performance, we benchmark in public through the community-standard SemiAnalysis InferenceX project.

Building on our initial submission of Qwen 3.5 on Ironwood TPU (TPU 7x), our engineering teams have further optimized the stack, bringing the lowest cost per million tokens overall to an industry leading 2.01 cents. Alongside these improvements, we have also published new state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance results to AgentX, the project's dedicated track for evaluating agentic long-context and multi-turn workloads. Ironwood TPU leads across most of the Pareto frontier. We look forward to continuously updating our public performance profiles as we bring more models and configurations to the leaderboard.

We did not build these backends in a vacuum. By embracing PyTorch and working directly with open-source project maintainers, we ensure these engines remain upstream-aligned and community-first:

This partnership is bringing SGLang's stellar team to build for TPU, delivering an engine that is already running in production at Meta and battle-tested at scale across demanding real-world scenarios.

Together, we integrated a high-performance Pallas megakernel for the 2.8T-parameter Kimi K3 model that runs the entire decode step as one kernel, serving more than 700 tokens per second to a single user on Ironwood TPU. Building on this work, Inferact recently led our first preliminary AgentX submission for Kimi K3 on the vLLM-TorchTPU stack. This initial milestone already demonstrates exceptional performance per TCO in ultra-high-interactivity workloads, and the rapid increase in the maturity of the vLLM and PyTorch ecosystem on TPU for doing new frontier OSS models bring-up, with follow-up submissions set to unlock even greater efficiency through larger scale prefill/decode disaggregation.

To foster continuous open-source contribution, vLLM is also launching a first-of-its-kind community contribution TPU capacity pool to provide free TPU compute to developers who actively contribute to the vLLM engine.

As the models get larger, we are evolving both engines to make large-scale TPU inference deployments performant and efficient. The major features for production-grade agentic workloads are already supported. More performance optimizations and advanced features are under way – open a Github issue to request collaboration on yours!

Across the two engines, most of the popular open model families are supported, including Qwen, DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi, GPT-OSS, Gemma and more. The team is investing in making more models available to run natively on TPUs, including Day 0 support for new open models. We also want to give the community the tools and TPU capacity to tune performance for their own workloads and configurations.

vLLM-JAX and SGLang-JAX remain important projects. Both will continue to be maintained, supported, and available for the community to use and adapt.

#10013. Bringing Visual Graph Debugging to Custom Edge Compilers with Model Explorer

Model Explorer goes beyond high-level model graphs. See how Arm plugs in custom compiler IRs, verifies NPU delegation side-by-side, and maps cycle-level profiling traces directly onto your execution graph.

Machine learning models run locally on a wide range of hardware, from low-power edge devices to gaming graphics and physical AI systems. Running models efficiently on these targets requires compilation steps such as quantization, graph lowering, operator fusion, and hardware delegation.

Arm used Google AI Edge Model Explorer to give developers visibility into these pipelines. With Model Explorer's hierarchical graph visualization and plugin architecture, Arm built several open-source adapters that make edge model transformations easier to inspect.

When deploying a model to edge hardware, a framework change or operator constraint can alter the exported execution graph. Engineers often need to answer three questions:

Answering these questions by reading raw flatbuffers or text logs takes time, especially for large language models (LLMs) and neural networks. Arm needed a visual tool to inspect Arm-specific intermediate representations and hardware profiling traces.

To address these deployment challenges, Arm developed custom adapters for Google AI Edge Model Explorer to support several model formats (i.e., TOSA, VGF, and PTE), establishing a comprehensive visual workflow for on-device optimization. Using these extensions, engineering teams can validate exported pipelines, verify accelerator delegation, and pinpoint cycle-level performance bottlenecks directly on the model graph:

Arm engineers used Model Explorer to validate a PyTorch-trained Neural Super Sampling (NSS) model exported through the ExecuTorch Arm backend as a VGF file for Vulkan ML Extensions. While inspecting the VGF graph, the team found unintended TRANSPOSE operators introduced by a change in the ExecuTorch Arm backend.

Model Explorer enables users to inspect individual nodes of the model graph, such as the rescale operator depicted below, which displays the operator's attributes and SPIR-V tensor connections. This functionality assisted the Arm team in identifying and resolving the regression without requiring manual analysis of raw log files.

To optimize vision models for accelerators like the Arm Ethos-U85 NPU, Arm engineers used Model Explorer's split-pane view to compare CPU and NPU-delegated graphs side-by-side for a Ultralytics YOLO model.

The split-pane view showed the structural difference: the CPU graph displays each individual layer, while the NPU graph groups the network into a single EthosUBackend block between quantize and dequantize nodes. For partially supported models in LiteRT or ExecuTorch, this view helps identify un-delegated operators and split subgraphs.

To find latency bottlenecks on the Ethos-U NPU, Arm ran their model on their Fixed Virtual Platform (FVP) simulator and used Model Explorer's node data plugin to overlay cycle-accurate execution traces onto the graph. Color-coded heatmaps showed that a single TRANSPOSE node was the main latency bottleneck.

You can use Google AI Edge Model Explorer along with Arm's open-source adapters today to inspect and optimize your own on-device models locally via PyPI or GitHub.

Special thanks to the contributors across the Arm and Google AI Edge teams for their work on these adapters and integrations:

Product manager: Charlie Stokes (ARM), Derek Bekebrede

Designers: Ami Kubota, Ioannis Politis (ARM), Kathleen Low, Philip Watson (ARM)

Senior Sponsors: Bala Gattu (ARM), Cormac Brick, Joe Alderson (ARM), Matthias Grundmann, Sharbani Roy (ARM)

#9995. Designing the hf CLI as an agent-optimized way to work with the Hub

hf is the official command-line entrypoint to the Hugging Face Hub. Anything you can do on the Hub from the Python SDK, you can do from your terminal: download and upload models, datasets and Spaces; create and manage repos, branches, tags and pull requests; run Jobs on HF infrastructure; manage Buckets, Collections, webhooks and Inference Endpoints.

The hf CLI has been primarily built for our users over the years. But it's now increasingly used by coding agents: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and more. So we rebuilt it to make it work for both audiences at once. This blog post summarizes what we did, and how we benchmarked it. We found that on complex, multi-step tasks the no-CLI baseline (an agent hand-rolling curl or the Python SDK) uses up to 6× as many tokens as the hf CLI.

We started tracking agent usage of the Hub in April 2026. The hf CLI (and the huggingface_hub Python SDK it's built on) detects when a coding agent is driving it by reading the environment variables agents set: CLAUDECODE/CLAUDE_CODE for Claude Code, CODEX_SANDBOX for Codex, plus Cursor, Gemini, Pi, and the universal AI_AGENT. That single signal does two jobs: it shapes the CLI's output (more on that below) and it tags each Hub request with an agent/ user-agent, so we can attribute traffic to the agent driving it. The two largest by distinct users are Claude Code and Codex, well ahead of everything else, and they're the two agents we benchmark later in this article.

The bars count distinct users per agent; request volume is the sub-label. Claude Code alone is ~40k users and nearly 49M requests, with Codex close behind. These are early numbers (we only began attributing agent traffic in April 2026), but the scale is already significant, and we expect it to keep growing as coding agents become a standard way to work with the Hub.

Humans and coding agents expect different outputs for the same hf commands. A human wants rich terminal output: ANSI color, padded tables truncated to fit the screen, a green ✅ on success, ✔ for booleans, progress bars, prose hints. An agent wants the inverse: no ANSI, nothing truncated, every value in full since an agent can handle far denser output than a human, kept compact and structured to stay light on tokens. It also can't answer a CLI prompt and will happily re-run a command after a timeout. The rest of this section is how hf gives each side what it needs. We introduced agent-mode output in hf v1.9.0 and have been migrating the rest of the CLI to it gradually in the following releases.

When hf auto-detects agent use (via the environment variables mentioned above), it renders the same command differently. It optimizes output format for humans or agents without passing a flag:

A human gets an aligned table, truncated to fit the terminal, plus a hint on how to see more, with color cues for status (a green ✓ on success, red on error). An agent gets the complete record as TSV: full repo ids, full ISO timestamps, every tag, no ANSI codes, nothing truncated, clean to parse and light on tokens.

In practice, we've implemented logging methods like .table(...), .result(...), .json(), etc., which take raw data as input and handle the formatting. In addition to human and agent modes, we've introduced --json and --quiet options to make it easier to pipe commands together. The default mode is automatically chosen based on context, but users can always force the format of their choice with --format human | agent | json | quiet.

CLI commands rarely run in isolation: one step usually implies the next (git add, then git commit). Many hf commands now end with a hint: the exact next command to run, pre-filled with the IDs you just used, so a user or agent can chain straight to the next step instead of working it out from scratch. Start a Job in the background and it points you to its logs; create a Space and it points you to its boot status:

For a human that's a convenience. For an agent it's a rail: the next action is named, parameterized with the right ids, and ready to run, so it takes fewer steps working out what to do. Errors behave the same way, naming the fix instead of just failing:

Hints, warnings and errors all go to stderr while data goes to stdout, so none of this guidance pollutes the output the agent is parsing.

hf never sits on an interactive prompt waiting for a key an agent can't press. A destructive command still asks a human to confirm, but in agent mode it fails fast with the fix in the message (Use --yes to skip confirmation.), and -y/--yes skips it. And because agents retry on timeouts and lost context, operations are built to be safe to repeat: hf repos create --exist-ok is a no-op if the repo already exists, and re-running an upload re-commits cleanly. Separately, the commands that move real data take a --dry-run that shows exactly what they'll transfer before they run, which proves handy for humans and agents alike, since neither has to commit to a long download or blind sync:

hf is built to be probed: run hf to see the resource groups, run --help on the one you need, and every --help ends with real, copy-pasteable examples (which an agent matches against far faster than it parses a description):

The command tree is consistent, resource + verb with the obvious aliases (hf models ls, hf repos create, hf jobs ps, hf collections delete; list/ls, remove/rm), so once an agent learns one command it can guess the rest. And the output composes: -q prints one id per line to pipe into the next command, --json gives you something to hand to jq.

To find out whether the hf CLI is really more efficient for agents, we measured it. We built a small evaluation harness and ran the same set of Hub tasks through each way of driving the Hub, many times over, grading every run against the live Hub. Here's the headline before the methodology: across both agents the hf CLI comes out ahead, most clearly on complex, multi-step tasks where it uses far fewer tokens.

(self-report error = the agent reported success on the 17 solvable tasks but the Hub said otherwise. The hf CLI rows are the CLI with its skill installed; what the skill adds on top of the bare CLI (chiefly fewer tool calls) is broken out in the skill section below. Representative transcripts are published in this bucket.)

We defined 18 non-trivial Hub tasks. Not "download a file", but the kind of thing you'd actually ask for: aggregate a trending org's models, inspect a repo's files and their sizes, upload a folder with include/exclude rules, delete files, copy files across repos, open a PR that adds a license, create a repo with a branch and a tag, sync and prune a bucket, build a collection. Each task goes to a fresh coding agent with exactly one way to talk to the Hub:

We run the hf CLI in two configurations, with and without its skill (a generated command reference we come back to in its own section). But the headline comparison below is simply hf CLI vs curl / the SDK; the skill's incremental effect is small enough that we break it out on its own rather than crowd it into the main results.

The config is deliberately clean: a fresh instance per run, no custom MCP servers, no CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md, nothing in context to nudge behavior. The task and the tool go into a single prompt, and the agent finishes with a TASK_COMPLETE or TASK_FAILED marker, but we don't trust that marker (an agent will report success on work that never landed), so we grade every run independently by re-querying the live Hub: did the branch really get created, is the file actually gone, does the bucket exist? Each task/tool combination is run 10 times, since coding agents are non-deterministic, about 520 runs per agent (18 tasks × 3 tools × 10 reps, minus a cap on one billable Jobs task) and ~1,000 graded runs in total. We ran the whole thing twice, on the two most popular coding agents (Claude Code with Sonnet 4.6 and OpenAI Codex with GPT-5.5).

The two charts below unpack the table above. First, task success on Sonnet, the agent where curl and the SDK struggle most:

Without the CLI, curl and the SDK trail by ten points, because on Sonnet they simply can't finish parts of the job (the writes, mostly), while the hf CLI clears them.

The second image shows token impact on GPT-5.5, broken down per task. Each bar is the curl/SDK tokens divided by the CLI's on the same task, so 2.4× means the non-hf version burned 2.4 times as many tokens to do the same thing:

On a one-shot read (count dataset rows, batch metadata) curl and the SDK are fine, and sometimes lighter. But as tasks get more complex and involve several dependent steps, the agent has to hand-roll the entire chain of REST calls (or dig through the SDK) and the cost blows up: 2.4× to 6× the CLI's on creating a repo with a branch and tag, deleting files, copying across repos, or syncing a bucket. The hf CLI lets the agent express the task as a few higher-level commands, rather than crafting a complex workflow.

hf ships a skill: a compact reference of the whole command surface that an agent loads as context. It's auto-generated from the live hf command tree, one line per command (its signature, a one-line description, and the flags that matter), grouped by resource, with a short glossary of common options. It deliberately skips the self-explanatory flags so it stays terse and light on context, and it's regenerated every release. Run hf skills preview to print it, or install it with:

What does it buy you? Mostly, the agent stops guessing. The clearest single view is how many commands each run takes, with the skill and without:

On both agents that's about ten commands per task down to about seven, roughly 30% fewer tool calls. That's because the agent isn't probing --help to find the right command and argument. The skill won't cut your token bill, because it prepends a fixed slice of info to the context, so tokens remain about the same or slightly tick up for the same task. The Skill won't make the CLI more reliable either, but it will help the agent spend time running your task rather than finding out how the tool works. This could be particularly helpful when using hf with local models.

We ran each task in a fresh session, so the skill pays its context cost on every task. In a real multi-task session that cost amortizes (the agent learns the command surface once), so the token picture likely improves there; we didn't measure that case.

We benchmarked all this because we think it matters. Agents are becoming real users of the Hub: they train models, build and clean datasets, and ship demos as Spaces, almost always on behalf of a person. A Hub that works well for agents is also a Hub that works better for the people using them. The better an agent's tools are, the more it can do for you.

If your agent interacts with the Hugging Face Hub, we recommend giving it the hf CLI:

Then hand it the skill, so it knows the whole command surface from the first turn:

Then point your agent at the Hub and let it work. Make sure you're logged in (hf auth login), then hand it a prompt like:

It'll work out the commands on its own and come back with something useful.

The full command reference lives in the hf CLI guide.

Building an agent harness? Get it registered! That's how hf learns to detect it, and how the Hub attributes its traffic to your harness. You simply need to open a small PR adding an entry to agent-harnesses.ts. Read the Register your agent harness guide for more details.

Giving AI agents access to command-line tools can make them more capable because they can interact with real development resources instead of relying entirely on generated text. The important part is setting appropriate permissions, defining task boundaries, and checking the results of commands before allowing consequential changes. I also think repeatable workflows make these integrations easier to manage, especially when the same development tasks occur frequently. This guide onhttps://mobisoftinfotech.com/resources/blog/ai-development/ai-workflow-automation-cursor-claude-commands is relevant to that idea, as reusable commands can help standardize routine coding activities. Combining tool access with clear safeguards is key to building dependable AI-assisted workflows.

#9992. Introducing the Microsoft Copilot harness in Foundry Agent Service

A model can reason about a task. Completing that task takes more: the right context, tools, execution environment, and controls, and an agent loop that brings them together.

Microsoft’s unified harness strategy brings a shared execution foundation across our agent experiences while preserving customer choice. In Microsoft Foundry, that means you can choose a supported model and decide how much of the agent stack to build yourself, without having to assemble every layer around it.

Today, we’re introducing the Microsoft Copilot harness in Foundry Agent Service in public preview. It gives developers a fully managed way to build agents that reason, use tools, and complete complex, long-running tasks. It’s our opinionated approach to helping agents complete complex work. We’re also announcing general availability of long-running resilience for hosted agents. Together, these capabilities help developers build more reliable agents for complex, long-running workflows.

Many teams building agents end up implementing the same execution machinery: coordinating model and tool calls, maintaining working context, managing files, and deciding how to continue when a task requires more than one step. That work matters, but it isn’t usually what differentiates your application.

The Copilot harness gives you a managed execution system for agents you define declaratively in Foundry Agent Service. Microsoft runs the agent loop and sandbox; you bring the knowledge, procedures, and tools that make the agent yours.

The public preview brings together four building blocks:

The harness manages working context as tasks develop and coordinates model and tool steps toward a requested outcome, within configured limits and policy boundaries. You choose a supported Foundry model without having to rewrite the orchestration around it.

That lets your team focus on improving the agent’s expertise and evaluating its results.

“With the Microsoft Copilot harness in Foundry Agent Service, we had a solution running in less than a week, allowing us to focus on design and capabilities instead of the infrastructure underneath it. That speed will help us bring our vision of AI that runs within and alongside our products to market faster.”

— Chris Evans, Chief Technology Officer, Confluence Technologies

“The Microsoft Copilot harness in Foundry Agent Service gives Fashable a powerful foundation for turning complex sourcing processes into governed, measurable agent workflows. We see the opportunity to generate complete tech packs from our knowledge and templates, while extending our A2A sourcing network beyond digitally connected suppliers through email and voice. Most importantly, we can equip brand and manufacturer agents with deeper knowledge and new capabilities to work across sourcing and negotiation without automating away accountability: agents can discover, engage and calculate, while commercially binding decisions remain under human control.”

Consider an agent that researches a topic, analyzes supporting data, and produces an evidence-backed brief. The same pattern can support market research, operational analysis, or an internal planning workflow: instructions define the outcome, skills define the method, and tools provide access to evidence.

Here’s a compact example using the preview Azure Developer CLI (azd) surface.

First, put a reusable procedure in skills/research-brief/SKILL.md:

Then describe the skill and agent in azure.yaml:

Set the referenced environment values, then deploy and invoke:

azd is one authoring option. You can also start in the Foundry portal or use Foundry Toolkit for Visual Studio Code. In the GitHub Copilot app, the Microsoft Foundry plugin and Microsoft Foundry Skill provide a conversational path to creating and managing prompt agents.

These options let you build on a managed harness. When your application needs a different framework or its own execution logic, hosted agents give you another path.

Hosted agents in Foundry Agent Service let you bring your own framework, agent loop, middleware, dependencies, and runtime behavior while Foundry manages hosting. Long-running resilience for hosted agents is generally available this week, helping agents recover from interruptions during work that takes hours or days.

Foundry detects interruptions and restarts the work with its original input. Your code saves progress and intermediate results so the agent can pick up where it left off. If the agent updates another system, your workflow also needs to prevent duplicate actions when work restarts.

For example, an agent analyzing a large dataset can save completed stages and resume from the last checkpoint. If it also creates a report in another system, it should check whether the report already exists before creating it again.

Foundry provides the recovery foundation; your application determines what to save and how to resume. Conversation history alone isn’t enough to restore work in progress.

These workflows have different requirements, and there isn’t one right level of abstraction for every agent. Foundry Agent Service lets you choose where to invest your engineering effort:

Start with the level that fits your application’s requirements, rather than taking ownership of infrastructure you don’t need to differentiate.

During this preview, select the Microsoft Copilot harness when creating the agent. Existing agents are unchanged, switching the harness after creation isn’t supported yet, and Foundry manages the execution environment’s CPU, memory, and idle settings.

You can start in the Microsoft Foundry portal or use azd to keep the agent definition alongside the rest of your application.

Pricing: Billing for the Copilot harness in Foundry Agent Service begins December 1, 2026, with consumption-based pricing. Harness runtime usage is free before December 1; model inference and separately billed tools and connected services remain subject to their applicable charges. Starting December 1, sandbox compute and memory are billed at USD $0.0994 per vCPU-hour and $0.0118 per GiB-hour, respectively. Prices may vary by region and agreement.

Jeff Hollan is the VP of Product for the Microsoft Foundry Agent Platform.

Viswajeeet is a Principal Software Engineer on Foundry Agents Team in CoreAI, where he leads managed agents platform. He also works on agent identity and toolboxes in Foundry to help customers’ agents achieve better outcomes with right set of controls.

Anthony is a product manager on the Microsoft Foundry team, focused on helping developers build and run AI agents. He works on Foundry Agent Service, making powerful agent capabilities easier to use without the overhead of managing the underlying infrastructure.

#9990. Migrating Your GitHub CI to Hugging Face Jobs

If you have a GitHub repository and you have GitHub Actions enabled, you probably use GitHub-hosted runners for CI. That is the default for many projects because it is simple: add a workflow, write runs-on: ubuntu-latest, and GitHub gives you a machine.

That default is convenient, but it also has limits. GitHub Actions can be slow or down for maintenance, the hosted machines are generic, and GPU access is not something most open-source projects can just turn on. For Trackio, those limits started to matter. We wanted both reliable CPU CI for basic unit tests and frontend checks, but also GPU CI for tests that need to run on actual CUDA hardware.

So built an alternative: keep GitHub Actions in charge of CI, but run the jobs on Hugging Face Jobs.

The result: Trackio's CI now runs on Hugging Face Jobs and streams back real-time logs, cutting our CI time for CPU jobs by about 30% and enabling a whole new test suite that runs on GPU machines!

In this article, we explain step-by-step how to recreate the same setup for your GitHub repo. If you are using an agent, you can point it to this article, since we provide CLI instructions alongside browser-based instructions for us humans.

Let's start with a quick intro to Hugging Face Jobs!

Hugging Face Jobs lets you run commands or scripts on Hugging Face's serverless infrastructure with almost any hardware flavor. A Job is essentially:

That makes Jobs a natural fit for CI. CI jobs are already command-driven, already run in clean environments, and often benefit from choosing exactly the right hardware. For ML libraries, the GPU case is especially compelling: you can run a test suite on real GPU hardware without maintaining your own always-on runner.

The key step is connecting GitHub Actions to HF Jobs, which we describe below.

For this setup, we created huggingface/jobs-actions, a small bridge that turns a GitHub Actions job into an ephemeral self-hosted runner running inside an HF Job.

From GitHub's point of view, this is just a self-hosted runner. From Hugging Face's point of view, it is just a Job that launches a container to run the workflow steps from the repo’s GitHub Actions.

The first thing you need is the dispatcher. This is a small Docker Space that receives GitHub workflow_job webhook events and launches HF Jobs in response.

Create this first because the GitHub App needs a webhook URL, and that URL comes from the Space. This Space should be under your own namespace or under a Hugging Face org that you have write access to.

Go to huggingface/jobs-actions-dispatcher and click Duplicate this Space.

Use cpu-upgrade for real CI so the dispatcher stays available for GitHub webhooks. cpu-basic is fine for testing and will probably work, but it can sleep after inactivity; if GitHub's webhook arrives while it is waking up, the workflow may stay queued forever.

After it builds, open the duplicated Space. You will see a section that says "Required Space secrets," which you can ignore for now. The landing page should display the GitHub App webhook URL you need in the next step. It will look like this:

If you'd prefer to set up the dispatcher Space with an agent or use a CLI workflow:

Next, create and install the GitHub App from the dispatcher Space itself. This App needs permission to listen for queued workflow jobs and create ephemeral self-hosted runner registration tokens.

In the setup form, enter the GitHub repo whose CI should run on HF Jobs:

Then click the button to create the GitHub App. GitHub will ask you to choose a name for the App; the name can be anything, as long as it is available in your GitHub account or org. After you submit, the final screen tells you exactly how to upload the App credentials to the dispatcher Space with the hf CLI.

Important note: you will need to provide an Hugging Face token that has permissions to launch Jobs, corresponding to your personal account or an org under which Jobs should be charged. This token should be saved as the HF_TOKEN secret in your dispatcher Space.

Finally, you will install the App on the same GitHub repo you entered in the Space. In the Trackio setup, we installed it on gradio-app/trackio.

The GitHub App manifest flow is still browser-based, but an agent can follow the same Space-driven path:

Paste $GITHUB_REPO into the Space, click the GitHub App creation button, choose any available App name, and follow the generated GitHub instructions.

After the App exists, install it on your repo from the App settings page. For a GitHub org, the installation settings are under:

At this point, the dispatcher Space should be configured. The GitHub App setup flow generated the commands that upload the App credentials, webhook secret, and Hugging Face token to the Space.

By default, HF Jobs are launched under the same namespace as the dispatcher Space. Optionally, set HF_NAMESPACE as a Space variable if you want to bill jobs to a different Hugging Face user or org:

The token you set in Step 2 should correspond to this namespace.

The actual workflow change is small. Instead of:

use one of the labels handled by the dispatcher:

For any GitHub Action you'd like to run on HF Jobs, this 1-line change is all you need!

To add a minimal smoke-test workflow from the CLI:

You should be able to see logs just like a regular GitHub Action—for example, in this Trackio PR #565.

Our first CPU setup used ubuntu:22.04 and installed missing system packages during every run. That worked, but it was slower than it needed to be. GitHub's ubuntu-latest image includes a lot of developer tooling by default; a bare Ubuntu image does not.

For Trackio, the UI tests need Playwright browsers, Node, ffmpeg, sqlite, git, and normal Linux build dependencies. Hugging Face Jobs supports using any Docker image, so we switched to the Microsoft Playwright image, which worked well:

Here are the numbers from the Trackio CI:

The biggest win was GPU CI. The Trackio GPU check ran on HF Jobs and passed in 45s, costing less than a cent at the t4-small rate for that duration.

The CPU result was also encouraging. With the right image, the Linux test job was faster than the GitHub-hosted baseline. That suggests HF Jobs can be a practical CI backend, especially for ML projects that need custom images or accelerators.

Logs were another pleasant surprise. GitHub Actions logs are useful, but the web UI can be heavy for large logs. HF Jobs logs are easy to fetch from the CLI:

That makes them easy to inspect with local tools or coding agents. In our bridge, we also mirrored the GitHub Actions job log into the HF Job log, so either system had enough information to debug a run.

Finally, although we didn't need them for Trackio's CI, HF Jobs also supports mounting volumes, which can be very helpful if you need to load datasets or models from Hugging Face quickly as part of your CI.

Hopefully, this gives you all you need to try HF Jobs for running your GitHub Actions!

#9989. How to Build a Typed AI Pipeline With Jev and Clairic.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A support email lands: "Order NW-47790, the tent poles snapped on the first night, I paid $389 and I want every cent back today or I'm disputing the charge."

To act on that, your code needs answers to a handful of small questions. Is it a refund request? How urgent is it? Should a person handle it? What's the order number? How much money is involved? It's the same problem whether you're sorting a support inbox or building a custom chatbot that has to work out what each customer is asking for.

The usual move is to send the whole email to a chat model with a prompt that ends "respond in JSON", then validate whatever comes back. It works, but you're paying a model built to write essays to fill in five fields, and you're parsing its guess at a schema.

System One models are built for exactly this kind of job. In this tutorial we'll build a small support inbox pipeline with two of them: Jev from TypeSafe makes the decisions, and Clairic from Cloudflare reads the values. Plain TypeScript then turns their answers into an action. No prompt engineering for output formats, and no JSON repair.

The name comes from Daniel Kahneman's Thinking, Fast and Slow. System 1 is the fast, intuitive kind of thinking you use to read a face or a sign. System 2 is the slow, deliberate kind you use for long division.

A System One model is an AI model that understands natural language but doesn't generate text. You give it some input (the state) and a set of typed questions, and it gives back typed answers with probabilities. There's no free text to parse, because the model can only answer in the shape you asked for.

That's different from asking a chat model for structured output. SitePoint's guide to LLM structured output with JSON Schema shows how to constrain a chat model and validate its JSON with Zod. With a System One model, the type is the interface: a yes/no question comes back as a probability, a pick-one question comes back as one of your options, and a date comes back as a date.

Jev and Clairic are both System One models, but they do different jobs, and that's what makes them a good pair.

Jev can't hand you an order number, and Clairic has no way to pick from a list of options or answer yes or no. Give each one the job it's built for.

If you've read SitePoint's Jev and LangChain tutorial, you've seen Jev deciding which model handles an agent's request. Here we'll use it on the incoming text itself.

Five made-up emails for a made-up outdoor gear store go in. For each one:

Both models read the same email, so they run at the same time.

Put the three values in your environment:

No SDKs are needed. Both models are a single fetch call.

Here's the test inbox. Each email is there to test a different path through the rules:

Jev takes a state (the email) and a set of named questions. We'll ask three, one of each type:

All three questions go in one request. Jev reads the email once and answers every question in parallel, so adding a question costs very little:

We pin jev-1.14.0 rather than the jev-latest alias. Your thresholds get tuned against one version's probabilities, so you want to choose when that version changes.

For the angry tent email, Jev came back with:

(Trimmed: the real response also includes the probability of every option and level.)

Clairic takes the same state, plus a set of typed fields instead of questions:

reference_date anchors relative dates like "the 14th" or "last Monday". In production, pass the date the email arrived.

Each answer comes back with three things worth using:

For the "where is it?" email, Clairic read the deadline like this:

"The 14th" became a full date, worked out from the reference date. Text fields like order_number also come back as character spans of the original email. The value is copied from the input, not generated, so it can't invent an order number that isn't there.

The two models don't depend on each other, so send both requests together:

The time for each email is whichever model is slower, not the two added together.

This is the part a chat model usually ends up doing badly: the business rules. Here they're ordinary code you can read, test, and change without touching a prompt:

Notice that the model's confidence sits right next to the business rule. A $18.95 refund is only automatic if Clairic is sure about both the order number and the amount. Raising the refund limit or the confidence bar is a one-line change, and you don't need to call either model again to see what it would do. Save the answers and replay them.

Every email went where it should. The whole run used 2,703 input tokens on Jev and 2,292 on Clairic, about US$0.0003 in total. At that rate, 10,000 support emails would cost roughly US$0.70.

The interesting part of the run wasn't the right answers. It was the two wrong ones.

"From last Monday." The run used 2 November 2026 as the reference date, which is a Monday. "Last Monday" means 26 October, but Clairic answered 2026-11-02, the reference date itself. Its confidence on that answer was 0.54, compared with 0.99 or higher on almost every other value in the run.

"A couple of weeks ago." Clairic turned this into 2026-10-19, which is a fair reading but still a guess. Its confidence was 0.43.

Neither date changed any action, because the rules only trust values at 0.9 or above. That's the habit to build: a value under your bar counts as unknown. A chat model returning JSON would have handed you "2026-11-02" with the same certainty as everything else.

One more catch: Clairic copied the order number as #NW-48213, hash included, because that's how the customer wrote it. Text values are spans of the input, so normalising them is your code's job. That's one line of code.

System One models handle the reading and the routing. They don't hold a conversation. Once an email is routed, something still has to write the reply, ask a follow-up question, or explain a returns policy in the customer's own words. That's where a chat model earns its cost.

The split that works is: System One models decide, code applies the rules, and a chat model only gets the cases where words matter.

We built a support inbox triage pipeline from two small models and some ordinary code:

Each email took about half a second and cost less than a hundredth of a cent. Most importantly, the two answers that would have been wrong came back flagged as unsure.

The full code is about 160 lines with no dependencies. Try adding a fourth Jev question (does the customer mention a photo?) or an estimate field in Clairic (how many days until the trip?), and see how little the rest of the pipeline has to change.

#9988. How an Agent Built a 3D Paris Gallery by Chaining Two Hugging Face Spaces

An agent built a 3D Paris gallery from two Hugging Face Spaces.

I asked a coding agent to build a beautiful website showcasing the monuments of Paris as 3D Gaussian splats. I never opened an image generator. I never touched a 3D reconstruction tool. The agent produced every asset (the images and the 3D splats) by calling two Hugging Face Spaces directly, then wired them into a cinematic viewer.

Here's the result, live as a static Space:

This post is about how that's possible now, and why I think it's a preview of how a lot of multimedia software gets built from here on.

Mitchell Hashimoto recently described a shift he calls the building block economy: the most effective path to software is no longer a polished monolith, but small, well-documented components that others (increasingly agents) can assemble. His key observation: AI is okay at building everything from scratch, but it is really good at gluing together proven pieces.

That thesis has mostly been told with code libraries. But the same forces are hitting multimedia AI. The hard part of using a state-of-the-art image model, a video model, a TTS model, or a 3D reconstruction model was never the model. It was the integration: SDKs, weights, GPUs, input formats, polling. If each model were instead a documented, callable block, an agent could glue them together the same way it globs together npm packages.

That's exactly what Hugging Face Spaces have quietly become.

The Hub hosts thousands of state-of-the-art models (a huge share of them open-weights), and most are deployed as interactive Spaces. As of now, every Gradio Space also exposes a plain-text agents.md that tells an agent exactly how to call it:

returns everything needed in one shot: the schema URL, the call and poll templates, how to upload files, and the auth hint:

No client library. No hardcoded integration. An agent reads that, and it can drive the Space end to end. Set an HF_TOKEN and you're going. You can find these instructions on any Gradio Space via its Agents button:

The real unlock is chaining: the output of one Space becomes the input to the next. Prompt → image → 3D. That's the whole pipeline behind this gallery.

The six source images the agent generated, all isolated on black, ready for single-image 3D reconstruction:

From there the agent did the "glue" work too. It noticed TripoSplat outputs are Y-down and flipped them upright, auto-framed each monument, compressed the .ply files to .ksplat (~3× smaller, so they load fast), built a Three.js viewer with a scroll-to-switch and drag-to-rotate UI, and deployed the whole thing as a static Space. The only human inputs were taste-level: "make it zoomed out," "replace the obelisk with something better for splatting," "the transition lingers too long."

Several of those steps were the agent reacting to reality. A wide glass pyramid splats poorly. A thin obelisk is dull. A single-view reconstruction infers the back. That is exactly the "outsourced R&D, fast iteration" loop the building-block economy predicts, except the R&D was a conversation.

The real test of a building block is how cheaply you can reuse it. Once this pipeline existed, spinning up entirely new galleries cost about one sentence each. "Create a similar Space with splats for Japan," then the same for Egypt, and the agent did the rest: six monument images, six splats, compression, a viewer, and a deployed Space, per country.

Several of those steps were the agent reacting to reality. A wide glass pyramid splats poorly. A thin obelisk is dull. A single-view reconstruction infers the back. That is exactly the "outsourced R&D, fast iteration" loop the building-block economy predicts, except the R&D was a conversation.

The real test of a building block is how cheaply you can reuse it. Once this pipeline existed, spinning up entirely new galleries cost about one sentence each. "Create a similar Space with splats for Japan," then the same for Egypt, and the agent did the rest: six monument images, six splats, compression, a viewer, and a deployed Space, per country.

Same two Spaces, same agents.md, only the prompts changed. That is the building-block economy in one line: the marginal cost of a new multimedia app falls toward the cost of describing it.

Point your own agent at a Space's agents.md and let it cook:

Paste either link into your coding agent (Claude Code, etc.), set your HF_TOKEN, and ask it to build something. The full, reproducible pipeline for this gallery, the scripts that hit those two agents.md endpoints, lives in the Space repo.

The building blocks are sitting right there on the Hub. The agents already know how to glue.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

When developers talk about high-performance mobile games, the Android NDK samples by Bruno Oliveira are often cited as the gold standard for clean, low-level C++. But as an iOS developer, I wanted to see if I could take that same “pure” C++ logic and make it sing on an iPhone.

My latest project, TunnelFeveriOS, is the result of that journey. It isn’t just a port; it’s a blueprint for building a custom game engine.

The original Endless Tunnel is built to live within the Android lifecycle (JNI, Activity, and NDK). Moving this to iOS required more than just hitting “compile.” I had to build a Platform Abstraction Layer.

To make the C++ engine talk to the iOS UI, I utilized Objective-C++ (.mm** files)**. This allowed me to keep the game's high-speed math and geometry in native C++ while using Cocoa Touch to manage the windowing and touch input. In TunnelFeveriOS, you’ll see how the view controller manages the game loop, feeding time deltas and touch coordinates directly into the C++ core.

Since the original game uses OpenGL ES, I leveraged iOS’s GLKit framework. The trick was ensuring that the shaders and vertex buffer objects (VBOs) originally written for Android were correctly initialized within the iOS EAGLContext. The result? 60 FPS performance that feels native because, at the machine level, it is.

A port is only “production-ready” if it handles modern app requirements. I integrated Google Mobile Ads (AdMob) to trigger Interstitial ads during game-over states.

This presented a unique threading challenge:

I implemented a messaging system that allows the C++ core to “request” an ad, which the Objective-C wrapper then catches and executes on the main thread — preventing the game from hanging or crashing.

This project proves that you don’t need a heavy engine like Unity or Unreal to achieve cross-platform results. By keeping the “brain” of your game in C++ and building thin “shells” for each platform (Android NDK or iOS/XCode), you gain:

If you’re interested in how to bridge the gap between low-level C++ and high-level iOS development, check out the full source code here:

Now that the foundation is laid, I’m looking into implementing a Metal-based renderer to fully embrace the future of Apple graphics. If you’ve worked on C++ to Metal bridges, I’d love to hear your thoughts in the comments!

#9986. Profiling in PyTorch (Part 2): From nn.Linear to a Fused MLP

This is the second post of Profiling in PyTorch, a series where we slowly build the skill of reading profiler traces and use it to drive optimization:

In the first part of this series "Profiling in PyTorch", we used torch.add(torch.matmul(x, w), b) to learn how to read PyTorch profiler traces. We also discussed several other topics that came our way - the CPU dispatch chain, launch overhead, the difference between an overhead-bound and a compute-bound regime, and some internals of torch.compile.

In the second iteration (this blog post), we climb one rung up the ladder. We replace the hand-written matmul-add pair with an nn.Linear (with bias=True). This is the building block every deep learning model uses. We then stack three of them (specific to our example), with an activation in between, to form a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) block.

The scripts for this blog post live here: 02_linear.py, 03_simple_mlp.py, and 03_kernels_mlp.py. Like before, it helps to open them in a separate tab and walk through the code as you read. We use an NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB GPU to run the scripts. It is really easy to set up a GPU on the Hugging Face infrastructure and experiment with the scripts using Dev Mode with Spaces. One could also run the scripts with the Hugging Face Jobs pipeline.

Before we begin, a quick recap of two ideas we will lean on repeatedly:

nn.Linear is a module wrapper around the same matrix multiplication and addition we already profiled in Part 1. The only difference is that it owns its weight and bias as parameters and exposes a forward method that PyTorch users have grown familiar with.

Where x is the input, w is the weight and b is the bias. Let's run 02_linear.py and check the profile.

trace-util is a utility that will sync your traces to a Hugging Face bucket and then provide the Preffeto URLs on your terminal.

Figure 1 shows the profiler trace of a forward call of the linear layer. We trace the forward call of the linear layer with a similar schedule setup as the previous traces, with wait=1, warmup=1 and active=3. This is why we see three Profile Steps in the CPU and GPU lanes.

If we zoom into the profiler trace, as we do in Figure 2, we notice an aten::t (transpose) op before the aten::addmm (multiplication and addition) op. We can already figure out that nn.Linear transposes the weight parameter and then multiplies it with the input. This is the reason we see an aten::t op.

An important thing to notice is that aten::t does not really copy or reorganize data: it only rewrites tensor metadata (shape and stride) on the CPU to represent the transposed matrix. It does not launch a kernel on the GPU. One can verify this two ways: by looking at the GPU lane in the trace, or by checking the aten::t row in the profiler table and the time it took on CUDA.

There is no aten::add (the bias addition) in the dispatch chain of the linear layer, as seen in Figure 3. This is because the bias addition has been folded into the matrix multiplication kernel, using what is called an epilogue.

An epilogue is a small computation that a GEMM (GEneral Matrix Multiply) kernel does at the very end, just before it writes its result back to HBM (High Bandwidth Memory, the GPU's main memory). Adding a bias, applying an activation, or scaling by a constant are all classic epilogues. The point of an epilogue is to avoid loading or writing to HBM a second time, since memory traffic makes an operation expensive.

nn.Linear calls torch.nn.functional.linear, which, in turn, calls aten::linear. aten::linear looks at the inputs, notices that a bias was passed, and dispatches aten::addmm(bias, x, weight) instead of doing a matmul and an add separately. addmm computes:

The cuBLAS GEMM kernel that runs on the GPU has a bias-add variant built in, and that's the kernel aten::addmm picks. The add never appears as a separate kernel because it is part of the matmul kernel's writeback, which is exactly what an epilogue is.

This is the moment to notice something subtle. The kernel you saw in Part 1 under --compile (addmm) is the kernel that eager nn.Linear already uses. There is nothing left for torch.compile to fuse here, which is the next thing we will verify.

Let's compile the forward call and look at the profiler trace. (The profiler trace is visualized in the next section)

If you compare the eager and compiled traces for a single nn.Linear's forward, you will find:

This is worth internalizing. A common reflex is to reach for torch.compile whenever a model feels slow. For a single GEMM-with-bias, compile has very little to do. This is not a bug, this is just that compile needs more than one operation to possibly do any fusing. Let's prove that by looking at an MLP.

A careful reader of the two traces (eager vs compile) will notice that the eager CPU dispatch chain has more in it than the compiled one.

The eager CPU dispatch chain inside aten::linear is aten::t followed by aten::addmm (Figure 4). To understand what aten::t actually does, we need a quick detour into strides and views.

A tensor stores its data as one flat, contiguous run of numbers in memory. The shape and stride are metadata that sit on top of that run and tell PyTorch how to walk it: a stride of (s0, s1) means "step s0 elements to move one row, step s1 to move one column". Change the metadata and you get a different view of the same raw data, with no copy:

M.t() did not move a single number. It returned a new view whose strides are swapped, so reading it row-by-row now walks the original buffer 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 in transposed order. The underlying data is identical; only the metadata differs.

This is exactly what aten::t does inside the linear layer: it does not allocate a new tensor or copy any data, it produces a view of the weight with rewritten strides.

As we can see in Figure 5, compile did not remove a GPU kernel: it removed the CPU overhead of dispatching that view. Inductor traced through the view chain at compile time, computed the resulting strides once, and emitted a direct aten::addmm call with those strides hard-coded. A few microseconds of CPU work disappear while the GPU does identical math.

As one would expect, when the input data violates the strides precomputed by the compiler, it will throw an error.

If you look at the GPU lane in both traces, there is exactly one kernel per forward, and it is the same kernel both times:

If no transpose kernel ran, who taught the GEMM to read the weight matrix in transposed order? The answer is in the kernel's name. Look at the suffix:

That tn is the layout descriptor. cuBLAS and CUTLASS precompile a separate kernel binary for each combination of input layouts.

n (non-transposed) and t (transposed) describe how a kernel walks its input during the inner loop. The dispatcher's job is to look at the input strides, decide which suffix combination matches, and pick the right precompiled kernel.

The kernel name in a profiler trace is a hash dump of the kernel's identity. If two runs show the same kernel name, the GPU is doing the same work. If they differ (e.g., _tn_ vs _nn_, bf16 vs fp16, or s16816gemm vs s161616gemm) then the GPU is doing different work, and the dispatcher took a different branch. Learning to read this name is one of the most useful habits when comparing traces.

In this section, we will profile a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP). To make this more interesting, we will profile a feed-forward network with the GeGLU activation variant (which is quite heavily used in practice). This is also our way of paying tribute to one of the greatest lines ever written in the history of deep learning research (Figure 6).

You will find the entire script here: 03_simple_mlp.py. Execute it like so:

Before we open the trace, let's think together about what we should expect to see. The forward function does a fair amount of computation, but most of it is already familiar to us.

We should expect three aten::linear dispatches, one for each nn.Linear layer. We should also expect two pointwise kernel launches, one for the GeLU and one for the multiplication. Forming this expectation before looking is the single most useful habit in the profiling journey: you read the trace to confirm or break a guess, not to form one from scratch.

From Figure 7 we can pat ourselves on the back, as our intuition was correct. Per forward pass (one mlp_fwd), the GPU runs exactly 5 kernels. Figure 8 highlights the "occupancy query" as seen in the CPU lane for the linear projection layers.

The three GEMMs each do an extra cudaOccupancyMaxActiveBlocksPerMultiprocessor call before the launch. We have a separate section on this in Part 1, you can find it here. That is cuBLAS sizing the grid. The pointwise ops (GeLU and mul) launch directly, with no occupancy query. So "a linear" is actually query + launch, while "a pointwise op" is just launch.

The aten::t, aten::transpose, aten::reshape, aten::view, aten::as_strided, and aten::_unsafe_view ops launch zero kernels. They show 0.000us of CUDA time in the table (Figure 9) because they only rewrite tensor metadata (shape and stride) on the CPU. A reader scanning the table sees around six op names per linear, but only one of them (mm) ever reaches the GPU.

The MLP flattens [batch, seq, dim] to [batch * seq, dim] for the matmul. In our command-line invocation we used 64 for batch and 128 for seq, so that's where the 8192 (batch * seq = 64 * 128) below comes from.

All three GEMMs have the same FLOP count, 2·8192·768·3072 ≈ 38.7 GFLOP each, yet down_proj is about 10% faster. Same work, different shape (N=768 instead of 3072), so cuBLAS picks a different tile (128×256, with a deeper stages_64x3 pipeline) that gets better reuse for that shape.

If you want to learn more about tiling in depth, here is a great resource to get started with.

This is exactly why the table had two GEMM rows (Figure 9): the 128x128 row is gate+up and the 128x256 row is down.

Before compiling the forward method and visualizing it, let's do the mental exercise again of asking ourselves what we expect to see in the trace. This is a fun experiment, and an important one to repeat every time you profile something yourself. Always build on your intuition, and the moment something does not match, stop and figure out why.

In eager mode, each nn.Linear was expanded into a chain of dispatcher ops (aten::linear → aten::t → aten::transpose → aten::matmul → aten::reshape → aten::mm). Those are the high-level wrappers that ATen walks through before reaching the real GEMM. torch.compile removes that chain.

By the time the compiled graph runs, there is no linear, no matmul, no transpose or reshape and those metadata ops were folded into how mm is called. We can see three bare aten::mm external calls (Figure 10). The proof that it is the same GEMM is that the kernel names are byte-for-byte identical to eager: ...128x128...stages_32x5_tn for gate and up, and ...128x256...stages_64x3_tn for down.

This is the headline of the whole compile lesson. The two eager pointwise kernels (GeLU and mul) plus a reshape collapsed into one kernel, triton_poi_fused__unsafe_view_gelu_mul_0 (Figure 11). Let's decode the name:

Why is this a win? In eager mode, the intermediate h = gelu(g) is a full [8192, 3072] bf16 tensor (around 50 MB) that the GeLU kernel writes to HBM and the mul kernel immediately reads back. Fusion keeps it in registers (memory that resides inside the chip and are closer than the HBM). The Triton kernel reads g and u once, computes gelu(g) * u, and writes the result once. One whole round trip of the intermediate through global memory is gone.

So far we have let PyTorch (eager) and the compiler (torch.compile) pick our kernels. Now we plug in a kernel that a human expert wrote and tuned by hand. We use the LigerGEGLUMLP layer, that we can easily fetch from the Hugging Face Hub with the kernels library.

The full script is here: 03_kernels_mlp.py.

Figure 12 shows the profile for the LigerGEGLUMLP layer using the Liger kernels from the Hub.

Writing kernels in Triton or CUDA is one problem and shipping them is another. The kernel has to be compiled for your exact combination of GPU architecture, CUDA version, and PyTorch version. This is the step that usually breaks ("works on my machine", missing nvcc, wrong Triton version).

The kernels library moves that build step off your machine. get_kernel("kernels-community/liger-kernels", version=1) downloads a pre-built, version-pinned kernel package from the Hugging Face Hub and caches it locally (here under ~/.cache/...kernels-community--liger-kernels). The benefits are:

When we say "tuned", we mean two concrete things, and both are visible in the trace.

The fusion is baked in. The LigerGEGLUMLP forward is down_proj(LigerGELUMulFunction.apply(gate_proj(x), up_proj(x))). The LigerGELUMulFunction runs a single Triton kernel, _geglu_tanh_forward_kernel, that computes gelu(gate) * up in one pass. This is exactly what we saw from torch.compile, where the intermediate never makes a round-trip through HBM. We get it here without the compiler, as shown in Figures 13 and 14 (no Dynamo guards, no compile latency, no recompilation risk).

The launch parameters were chosen for the hardware. The kernel does not guess its block size at random. Liger's calculate_settings picks them from the column count.

It is worth being honest about the trade-off here, because the raw numbers can be misleading. The Liger kernel runs in 92.8 µs, while Inductor's fused kernel from the compile run was 89.4 µs. At first glance the hand-written kernel looks slightly slower, but that comparison hides the cost that makes it worthwhile.

torch.compile specializes for a static shape. Inductor's 89.4 µs kernel is fast precisely because it was generated for this exact [8192, 3072] problem. Change the batch size, the sequence length, or the hidden dimension, Dynamo re-traces, and you pay the compile cost all over again to get a new specialized kernel.

So the real choice is not "slow human kernel vs fast compiled kernel". It is a fast generic kernel vs a kernel specialized for one particular input shape. The Liger kernel takes one set of launch parameters and runs them for any shape with no recompilation. It gives up the last few microseconds that per-shape specialization would buy, in exchange for being robust to changing shapes.

The table below collects what each step changed on the GPU and what it left untouched.

If there is one habit to carry forward, it is the one we practiced before every trace: guess first, then look. State what you expect the trace to contain, open it, and treat any mismatch as the most interesting thing on the screen.

This was the second stop in the Profiling in PyTorch series. In the next post we will keep climbing the ladder, moving from this MLP block towards the attention block and, eventually, a full model.

Thanks to Noe Flandre and Pedro Gabriel Gengo Lourenço for their reviews on the early draft of the post!

#9985. How Product Teams Can Use AI User Research to Test Assumptions Before Sprint Planning

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Sprint planning is on Thursday, and the top of the backlog rests on three things nobody has checked. Users want the feature, they will find it, and they will understand what it does when they do. Each belief is plausible, and each has already been written into a ticket.

AI user research uses language models to simulate or analyze user conversations, so a team can put a question to a modeled audience in minutes instead of recruiting people for weeks. Used well, it gives a product team a cheap first check on backlog assumptions. Used badly, it produces confident-sounding agreement. This guide covers a two-day routine that gets the benefit and avoids the trap.

An assumption is worth testing when the plan depends on it and a wrong answer would change the ticket. "Users like clean interfaces" fails that test. "Analysts re-apply the same filters every session" passes, because if it is false the saved-filters feature shrinks or disappears.

The timing matters because planning leaves little room for research. The Scrum Guide says Sprint Planning is timeboxed to a maximum of eight hours for a one-month Sprint, and the first question the team answers is why the Sprint is valuable. Checks run before that meeting inform the answer. Checks run during it eat the time meant for deciding.

Write each risky item as a short card that names the belief, the consequence of being wrong, and the decision it feeds. A card forces the team to say what would change its mind, which most tickets never do. Here is an example:

Aim for three to five cards. A team that tries to test the whole backlog will test none of it, and the cards on the riskiest items give the best return.

AI user research comes in two forms. The first analyzes data you already hold: clustering support tickets and summarizing interview transcripts. It works on real evidence, so its main risk is a sloppy summary.

The second form interviews simulated people. AI user research of this kind builds a panel of modeled personas matched to your target profile, asks them your questions, and reports the themes. It needs no recruiting and returns results quickly, which fits a two-day window. Its output comes from a model of users and not from users, and that distinction should appear in every planning document that cites it.

A simulated audience helps most when you want to sharpen a question, and least when you need proof. Nielsen Norman Group's 2024 review of synthetic users found them useful for generating hypotheses and preparing interview guides. It warned against using them for final decisions or concept validation, and for niche populations, because AI tends to please and "every idea is often seen as a good one."

Spend Tuesday collecting answers and Wednesday reading them skeptically. On Tuesday, put each card's question to the modeled audience in neutral wording, and ask what would make them not use the feature. A question phrased as "Would saved filters help you?" invites a yes, while "Walk me through setting up your weekly report" does not.

On Wednesday, compare the answers with what you already know from support tickets and analytics. Mark each assumption as supported, contradicted, or unclear. Treat a unanimous answer with suspicion, because real audiences rarely agree on anything. Also be wary of lists in which the modeled users "seem to care about everything," which is how Nielsen Norman Group describes their weak prioritization.

Whatever stays unclear or high risk goes to real people. Jakob Nielsen's classic analysis found that five users find about 85% of usability problems, assuming comparable users, and he recommended several small rounds over one large one. An AI check is a good way to decide what those five people should be asked.

Each mark maps to a different decision. A contradicted assumption means the ticket is cut or reduced to its smallest useful version. A supported assumption that rests only on simulated evidence is not yet safe, so schedule a real-user check as the first task in the sprint, ahead of the build work that depends on it. An unclear assumption should not receive full scope.

The cost of skipping this step is real. A 2019 analysis of 615 product subscriptions by a product analytics vendor found that about 12% of features generate 80% of daily usage volume, and 80% of features are rarely or never used. That is one vendor's customer base, and the figures cover features that customers chose to track, so treat them as a rough guide. They still suggest that most of a backlog is a bet.

AI user research cannot replace talking to real users. Nielsen Norman Group found that synthetic users gave overly optimistic accounts of their own behavior, such as claiming to finish every course in a study, and that they cannot supply real past experience. It also called presenting synthetic findings as real-user findings "an unethical way to share what you've learned."

Two habits keep a team honest. Label every piece of evidence in the planning document as modeled, observed, or reported, and require that any feature built on modeled evidence has a real-user check scheduled. The review also warned that teams starting with synthetic research may get comfortable and skip the real kind, so put the real check on the calendar before the first AI result arrives.

Can AI user research replace interviews with real users? No. It is a cheap first pass that helps you write better questions and spot weak assumptions. Anything that drives a significant build still needs real people.

How many assumptions should a team test before planning? Three to five. Pick the ones where a wrong answer would cut or reshape a ticket.

How do I stop simulated users from just agreeing with me? Use neutral, open questions, ask what would make them avoid the feature, and treat unanimous answers as a warning sign.

What should I do with results I cannot verify? Mark them as modeled, give them less weight than observed evidence, and schedule a real-user check before committing full scope.

Sources: Scrum Guide, Sprint Planning; Jakob Nielsen, "Why You Only Need to Test with 5 Users" (March 18, 2000); Nielsen Norman Group, "Synthetic Users: If, When, and How to Use AI-Generated 'Research'" (June 21, 2024); 2019 Feature Adoption Report (615 product subscriptions, vendor-reported).

#9984. What’s !important #17: Custom Highlight API, CSS Navigation Matching, Fixing text-stroke, and More

Plus, how to style skeleton UIs, how to enable diagonal scrolling, how images can overflow themselves, and yet, still more. Basically, how to do a lot of really cool (CSS) stuff.

Sunkanmi Fafowora demonstrated how to use the CSS Custom Highlight API, which is now supported by all major web browsers. Despite “CSS” being in the name (the styling is handled by the ::highlight() pseudo-element function), it’s actually JavaScript that makes the wheels go round for this one.

Both syntaxes are quite fun to work with, though.

If you’re curious as to how ::highlight() works alongside other highlight pseudo-elements (there are actually quite a few of them), I wrote something up not too long ago.

Temani Afif explained how images can sort of overflow themselves, because the element is like a container that the ‘replaced content’ (the image resource) can overflow.

I suppose that explains why we can swap the src using CSS, like this:

Temani also showed us what we can do with this information:

Tyler Sticka reminded us (well, I’m learning about it for the first time…) how to fix text-stroke with paint-order. For those who don’t know, text-strokes are center-aligned, so half of the stroke appears on the outside while the other half appears on the inside, and the inside half often looks terrible.

The paint-order property doesn’t fix the alignment, but it does ensure that the text fill is painted over the inside half of the stroke.

Also, the prefixed version of text-stroke (-webkit-text-stroke) is still necessary for all browser vendors. Overall, an upgrade for text-stroke is long overdue, and hopefully we see that soon.

Lea Verou contemplated how to style skeleton UIs using only CSS, and the wonderful CSS community chimed in with more than a few awesome solutions too. It was so nice to see box-decoration-break: clone in there (suggested by Agustin Capeletto), although different elements need different solutions, it seems.

Until it dawned on me: thick text-decoration + color: transparent + masks! Demo: codepen.io/leaverou/pen… But I can't for the life of me figure out how to round the edges (without HTML changes or fragility like hardcoding text size/length). Any takers?[image or embed]

Ahmad Shadeed showcased different ways to use the lh unit, which, as it turns out, has a range of uses. If you’re not familiar, 1lh is equal to the computed line-height.

Bramus explained how the new scroll-axis-lock property facilitates diagonal scrolling (the default behavior only allows for scrolling one axis at a time).

Bramus also unveiled CSS navigation matching, which basically enables us to style elements based on where the user is navigating to or from. (We have an early look at it as well.)

It’s kind of mind-blowing, to be honest. Bramus actually published this right after I wrote What’s !important #16 (the last issue), but I just couldn’t let this one fly under the radar…

Since neither Chrome, Safari, nor Firefox has shipped a new stable version since What’s !important #16 (and because it’s Friday), let’s wrap this one up early. Instead, I’ll leave you with an interesting question — what’s the worst HTML element?

#9983. Dark mode toggles: two states are enough

Exactly the kind of nerdy UI/UX discussion I love:

Lea’s pushing back on light/dark mode implementations that display three state options for visitors:

[…] a good two state control can actually express all three states — users just need to apply the override the first time it becomes relevant.

The first figure succinctly illustrates the point:

In short: No preference? Fall back to the system settings and provide a setting to override that if that’s needed/preferred. Then that preference is stored in localStorage for future sessions.

Something I sorta missed the first time I saw the image is that perhaps we don’t even need to display two states when we know what color scheme is active:

Personally, I’m convinced. Less UI that accomplishes the same as more UI is generally a good thing. Lea’s point goes way beyond that, getting into well-considered reasons that go beyond simplicity.

An interesting consideration is what happens when toggling back to a state. Like, if we start with a Light system preference, toggle it to Dark, then back to Light. Do we get a new override preference or go back to the system setting would be an undefined localStorage value? Maybe it doesn’t matter because theme switching isn’t exactly the primary user intent:

Remember, this control is entirely tangential to the actual user goal for visiting the website. Even if their intent were to pin light instead of reverting to System (light), this is something they would only notice once these diverge, i.e. the OS switches to dark. At that point, fixing it is a single click away. It’s such an easy fix, that there is no point in dwelling on it further.

To be clear, Lea is referring to persistent UI. The guidance is targeting toggles that are always visible to the visitor. That’s really, really common in a site’s header/navigation (my personal site included). If that’s the pattern, then it could distract from the visitor’s primary intent. And the more options we see, the more cognitive dissonance is introduced.

I think there’s an even more compelling argument in the thread:

All I ever wanted was for my OS to be dark, not every website I look at. It was a huge leap by the browser vendors to tie all web content to that system preference.Anyway, I think the light/dark preference should be in the browser, and what you propose seems perfectly in line with that.

Yes, please! Development for the preference, but no need to show an override when the setting is in the browser itself. Then a tri-state toggle might be more acceptable.

Speaking of which, Lea does offer two scenarios where three states make sense:

Update: Lea has published a follow-up that summarizes the whole discussion her first post stirred up. What’s left to say? It’s that this guidance is purely for persistent toggles, such as those in a main navigation. If that’s the case, then her two-state pattern is the way to go. But the best solution? Maybe no toggle at all and let the system default do the work.
